source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-10-09, from the ABFM 2025 In-Training Examination critiques, items 89 to 100. Each question cites its item. Authoring batch for the ITE pool; review before trusting.

questions.q: A 5-year-old fell off a table, vomited once, has a parietal haematoma and a normal examination. What is next?
d: CT of the head and neck
questions.why: A mild traumatic brain injury. Routine imaging is not recommended in children, and skull films have no role at all.

questions.q: After a child's minor head injury, what would make CT appropriate?
questions.a: Worsening symptoms or signs of headache
d: A single vomit at the scene of the fall
A scalp haematoma with nothing else
Being under six years old at the time
questions.why: A suspected head or neck injury on examination is the other trigger. A child who becomes fussier or holds the head has changed category.

questions.q: What would prompt a child protection referral after a fall at home?
questions.a: Delay in seeking care or inconsistent findings
d: Any fall from a piece of household furniture
A parietal haematoma after the fall
A parent who did not see the fall happen
questions.why: Unusual physical findings or behaviour between parent and child count too. A witnessed climb and fall, brought in straight away, does not.

questions.q: A motivated smoker asks for behavioural help to quit. Which change improves his chances?
questions.why: Part of the Ask, Advise, Assist model. Hypnotherapy and acupuncture lack moderate-quality evidence; caffeine and menthol have no role.

questions.q: Which pharmacotherapies are recommended for smoking cessation?
questions.why: Combining a drug with behavioural support beats either alone.

questions.q: What is the initial inhaler for COPD in GOLD group A?
d: An inhaled corticosteroid with a LABA
A LAMA, LABA and inhaled corticosteroid
questions.why: A long-acting beta-agonist is the alternative for group A. The combination is where groups B and E start, and triple therapy is considered for group E with eosinophils of 300 or more.

questions.q: Confused and hypotensive: glucose 750, osmolality 350, trace ketones, pH 7.3, normal gap. What is this?
questions.why: No significant ketosis and no acidosis. Isotonic fluid comes first, then an insulin infusion, with potassium added after the first bolus.

questions.q: At what rate is the insulin infusion run in the hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state?
questions.why: Half the ketoacidosis rate. Bicarbonate is considered only if the arterial pH falls under 7.0.

questions.q: What is the effect of adding a calcium channel blocker in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
questions.a: No mortality benefit, and possibly worse outcomes
d: Fewer admissions but no mortality change
questions.why: A thiazide is likewise an adjunct for congestion only. The drug that does cut mortality in HFrEF regardless of diabetes is an SGLT2 inhibitor.

questions.q: Two weeks of polyuria and polydipsia and a random glucose of 210. What else is needed to diagnose diabetes?
questions.a: Nothing; the symptoms and one value suffice
d: A repeat random glucose on another day
A fasting glucose on another day
A haemoglobin A1c to confirm it
questions.why: Without classic symptoms, a fasting value, an A1c or a 2-hour tolerance test each needs a second abnormal result to confirm.

questions.q: What does a 1-hour value of 145 mg/dL on a 50-g glucose challenge mean?
questions.a: A positive first step of gestational screening
d: Diabetes, needing no confirmation at all
Nothing; it is within normal limits
questions.why: The 50-g test belongs to pregnancy. Outside it, 100 to 125 fasting or an A1c of 5.7% to 6.4% is prediabetes.

questions.q: Six weeks after a casted forearm fracture: burning pain, pain to light touch, a warm swollen arm, weak grip. Cause?
questions.why: A clinical diagnosis by the Budapest criteria. No fever argues against infection, and no stocking-glove pattern against neuropathy.

questions.q: Which findings after limb trauma support complex regional pain syndrome?
a: A temperature difference between the limbs
questions.why: Objective findings are what separate it from factitious and functional disorders.

questions.q: Lower abdominal pain, cervical motion and adnexal tenderness, pus in the discharge, not pregnant. What test is added?
questions.why: Pelvic inflammatory disease is a clinical diagnosis in most cases, treated empirically once STI testing is sent. Laparoscopy is never the initial evaluation.

questions.q: Which findings on their own justify treating a woman at risk for pelvic inflammatory disease?
questions.why: Any one of the three. The others support the diagnosis without being required for it.

questions.q: What would prompt pelvic ultrasound in suspected pelvic inflammatory disease?
questions.a: Unilateral pain or an adnexal mass
questions.why: Those point to tubo-ovarian abscess or appendicitis. MRI follows if the ultrasound shows an abscess; CT looks for complications above the pelvis.

questions.q: A high-risk TIA 20 hours ago, ABCD2 of 4, normal examination. What is given on day one?
questions.why: The loading doses, within 24 hours of onset, then both drugs daily before dropping to one. Ninety-day stroke risk falls from 7.8% to 5.2% against aspirin alone.

questions.q: Which elements make up the ABCD2 score for a transient ischaemic attack?
questions.why: A score of 4 or more marks the attack as moderate to high risk, which is what earns the double antiplatelet course.

questions.q: Hepatitis C with fibrosis on ultrasound, in recovery from opioid use. What is begun now to improve the fibrosis?
questions.why: Antibiotic prophylaxis and beta-blockers have their own triggers, prior peritonitis and significant varices among them, and neither reverses fibrosis.

questions.q: Why raise HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis with a patient who has hepatitis C and a history of injecting?
questions.why: Offering both together improves uptake, but the prophylaxis itself does nothing for the liver.

questions.q: Pelvic pressure, mild stress leakage, anterior prolapse 0.5 cm above the hymen, only mildly bothered. What is advised?
questions.why: Training reduces prolapse by 1 to 2 cm and improves symptoms. Oestrogen alone has no clear evidence, and surgery can worsen incontinence, so it waits for more bother.

questions.q: A prolapse within how far of the hymenal ring, above or below, is grade 2?
questions.why: Prolapse tends to progress until menopause and then alternate between regression and progression.

questions.q: An hour of sudden leg pain, a cold numb mottled foot, no pedal pulses. What is the first step?
questions.a: Transfer to an emergency department with vascular surgery
d: Stat duplex ultrasonography of the leg
Stat CT angiography of the leg
questions.why: Imaging locates the block but must not delay the transfer. Skeletal muscle survives four to six hours without flow.

questions.q: Which anticoagulant is started on arrival for acute limb ischaemia?
questions.why: A direct oral anticoagulant has a place in chronic symptomatic peripheral artery disease, not in the acute event.

questions.q: Which are among the six Ps of acute limb ischaemia?
questions.why: Paralysis is the late one, and the one that means muscle is dying.
